summary.title: How to write an emulator (CHIP-8 interpreter)
summary.one_liner: You learn the basics of emulation and how to build a CHIP-8 interpreter in C/C++, covering the fetch-decode-execute cycle, memory, registers, timers, graphics, and keypad input.
keywords: how does a cpu execute opcodes
takeaways: Emulation runs the original machine code of a system, while simulation re-implements the behaviour of a game or program.
CHIP-8 is a virtual machine with 35 two-byte opcodes, 4K memory, 16 eight-bit registers, a 64x32 display, a 16-key hex keypad and two 60 Hz timers.
Each emulation cycle fetches two bytes at the program counter, merges them with bitwise OR, decodes them with switch statements, and executes them.
Sprite drawing (0xDXYN) uses XOR and sets VF on pixel collision; only 0x00E0 and 0xDXYN should set the draw flag.
The author suggests next steps such as Super CHIP-8, function pointers instead of a big switch, and a Gameboy (Z80) emulator.
summary.summary: The article is a hands-on guide by a multitouch/HCI researcher who has worked on emulators such as PCSX2, Dolphin and nullDC. It first explains what an emulator is compared with a simulator, then describes the CHIP-8 virtual machine's specifications: memory map, registers, stack, graphics, timers and keypad. It walks through the emulation cycle with C/C++ code samples for fetching, decoding and executing opcodes, including examples for 2NNN, 8XY4, FX33 and DXYN, and it includes the fontset and a game loop skeleton. The author links to a reference implementation (myChip8) and lists suggestions for further projects.
